title: Mindfulness of the body
hook: like a heavy stone ball thrown on wet clay, or a full water jar tipped

segments.voice: Yesterday: anapanasati, sixteen steps, and your line, the breath does it all.

It's after the meal, and a group of monks is sitting in the assembly hall, talking. It's wonderful, one of them says, how the Buddha calls mindfulness of the body a thing of great fruit. They're still talking when the Buddha walks in and asks what they were discussing. So he tells them himself. The hundred and nineteenth discourse is that answer, and near its end come pictures you can almost hold: a stone ball, a lump of wet clay, a water jar on a stand.
screen: `AFTER THE MEAL, IN THE HALL.` → `THE BUDDHA ASKS: WHAT'S THE TALK?` → `A STONE BALL. WET CLAY. A WATER JAR.`

segments.voice: Mindfulness of the body, kayagatasati, starts simply. Knowing the breath. Knowing the posture: walking, standing, sitting, lying down. Acting with full awareness, whether you're stretching an arm or chewing food. Then reviewing the body's parts, its elements, its mortality. Then the absorptions, with pictures: rapture and ease soaking through the body like water kneaded into bath powder, until no part is dry. Then the Buddha says something large. Whoever has developed mindfulness of the body has within it all the good states that lead to true knowledge, the way someone who pictures the great ocean includes every river that runs into it. Now the images. If you haven't developed it, it's like throwing a heavy stone ball onto a mound of wet clay: it sinks right in. That's how Mara, the tempter, finds a way in. Or like an empty water jar: anyone can pour water into it. But if you have developed it, it's like a light ball of string thrown at a door of solid wood. It bounces off. Or a jar already full to the brim: there's no room to pour anything in. And tip a full jar on its stand, and the water flows out wherever you choose: the mind can turn toward any of the higher knowledges. The text lists ten benefits, from enduring heat, cold and harsh words to freedom itself. All starting from a body you already have.
screen: `BREATH, POSTURE, FULL AWARENESS` · `EVERY RIVER INTO THE OCEAN` · `STONE BALL OR BALL OF STRING` · `THE FULL JAR, TIPPED AT WILL` · then, large: `THE BODY IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Let gravity have you, and feel where you meet the chair or the floor: the pressure under your thighs, your feet, your hands resting. You aren't trying to relax, just to know you're here, sitting. When the mind drifts, come back to weight and contact, like a full jar with no room for much else.
Kayagatasati. Mindfulness of the body: knowing breath, posture and action, so the mind is like a full jar that nothing can pour into.
Your line: the body is enough. A full jar leaves no room for anything else. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada and other Buddhist teachers often begin meditation with awareness of the body, including breath, posture and walking meditation, and some monastics contemplate the parts of the body as part of their training.

fork.setup: a jar is full to the brim. someone comes to pour more water in. what happens, in the Buddha's picture?
options: there's no room, so it can't be poured in.
fork.reveal: the full jar has no room. so the mind filled with body mindfulness gives distraction no place to enter.

original.note: Pali kayagatasati: mindfulness directed to the body. the title of MN 119.

trapdoor: what you thought: body awareness is the warm-up before real meditation.
what it means: MN 119 says it holds every good state leading to knowledge, as the ocean holds every river.
what a scholar hears: the Kayagatasati Sutta reuses the body contemplations of the Satipatthana Sutta and adds the jhana similes and Mara-access similes, ending with ten benefits.
recall: a monkey, caught by its own grip

chat.says: Why would a Buddhist teacher focus so much on just the body?
options: Developed well, body mindfulness holds every good state, like rivers in the ocean.
Because body work is simply easier than mind work for beginners.
Because a fit, strong body makes the mind calm without other practice.
chat.meaning: In MN 119, whoever develops mindfulness of the body includes all the good states leading to knowledge, as the ocean includes every river.

Mara.meaning: the tempter, who looks for a way in

absorptions.meaning: jhanas: deep, settled states of meditation

higher knowledges.meaning: special understandings a well-trained mind can turn toward

notes: MN 119 paraphrased. In the sutta the similes are framed as Mara finding or not finding an opportunity; the script says 'distraction and temptation find their way in'. Confirm this is a fair simplification.
